Archimedes' Angle Trisection

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This drawing shows a way to cut an angle into three equal pieces.
How to play: Drag B around the circle to choose the angle, then slide C along the line until D lands on the circle. You can also focus a dot and use the arrow keys.
Look for the math

For hundreds of years people tried to split an angle into three equal parts using only a straightedge and a compass; it cannot be done. Archimedes found a way if you are allowed to slide a marked ruler. Move the two dots and watch what happens when the marked point D reaches the circle.

A segment as long as the radius

The circle has centre O and radius R. A is the point on the right, and B is the dot you drag around the circle; the angle to cut is angle AOB. The other dot, C, slides on the line through O to the left. D sits on the ray from C towards B so that CD = R, exactly the length of OB. That is the mark on the sliding ruler, and it is why this is called a neusis construction.

Why a third appears

Suppose D has reached the circle, so OD = R as well. Then triangle CDO is isosceles: write its two equal base angles as q. By the exterior angle theorem the angle at D next to it is 2q. Triangle OBD is isosceles too, because OB = OD = R, so its angle at B is also 2q. Now look at triangle COB: its angles at C and B are q and 2q, so the exterior angle at O is q + 2q = 3q. But that exterior angle is angle AOB. Hence angle DCO = q = angle AOB / 3, exactly as Archimedes claimed.

Where C has to sit

The sliding dot is not free once the angle is chosen. If angle AOB = t, the isosceles triangle CDO has base OC = 2R cos(t/3), so C must be that far to the left of O. The logic test checks this for every whole angle from 1 to 179 degrees and for 200 random angles, and compares every step with a second transcription of the applet's own integer arithmetic.

One honest caveat: the applet rounds its points to whole pixels and calls D "on the circle" when OD is within 0.6 pixels of R. D can also land there by collapsing onto B (when CB = R and the angle is past 90°); that is a real second solution of the slide, but angle DCO is then not a third. The page's claim holds for the non-degenerate placement, where D and B are different points, and the status line says so when the collapsed one is reached. The cut-the-knot article describes this Java applet but now shows a GeoGebra remake of the same figure, so the rules followed here come from the Java code.

Try 120°: the third is 40°, and C lands about 1.7 radii to the left of O. Then drag B past 150° and see how hard the true solution becomes to find with whole-pixel steps.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
